objectives: Predict-then-match Words-in-Context to beat the familiar-meaning trap
Answer purpose/structure questions with a functional verb
Pin each author's stance before Cross-Text comparison

slides.title: Part 1 — From 'what' to 'how & why'
slides.body: Craft & Structure (~28% of Reading & Writing) stops asking what a text says and starts asking how it's built and why the author made each move.

slides.title: The question types
slides.body:
- **Words in Context:** which meaning does this word carry *here*?
- **Text Structure & Purpose:** what is this sentence/paragraph *doing* for the whole text?
- **Cross-Text Connections:** how would author 2 respond to author 1?

All three reward reading for *function*, not just content.

slides.title: Words in Context is not a vocabulary quiz
slides.body:
> **Key idea:** the SAT tests the word's meaning *in this sentence*, not its most common dictionary sense.

A familiar word with a secondary meaning is the most common trap. Cover the choices, predict a word that fits the sentence's logic, *then* match — don't pick the definition you'd give cold.

slides.title: Part 2 — Strategy a top scorer uses
Predict before you peek
slides.body: For Words in Context: read the sentence, mentally insert a blank, and predict your own word from the surrounding logic (contrast cues like *however*, cause cues like *because*). Only then read the choices and pick the closest synonym to *your* prediction. This neutralizes the 'familiar but wrong sense' trap.

slides.title: Purpose questions: name the verb
slides.body: For 'the main purpose of the underlined sentence is to ___', answer with a *verb*: to qualify, to counter, to illustrate, to concede, to transition. If you can name what the sentence *does* for the paragraph, the right choice is obvious and the 'true but not the purpose' traps fall away.

slides.title: Cross-text: pin each author's stance first
slides.body: Before comparing two short paired texts, write a 3-word stance for each (e.g., "pro, with caveats" / "skeptical"). Most questions reduce to: would author 2 *agree, qualify, or reject* author 1's specific point? Decide stance first; the answer follows.

slides.title: Part 3 — A worked example, end to end
Words-in-Context item
slides.body: Sentence: "The committee's *qualified* support meant the proposal advanced, but only after major revisions." Stem: as used, *qualified* most nearly means: (A) certified (B) limited/conditional (C) skilled (D) eligible.

slides.title: Walking it
slides.body: Predict from logic: "but only after major revisions" signals support that is *not full* → 'limited/conditional'. (A) certified and (C) skilled are common senses of *qualified* — classic familiar-meaning traps. (D) eligible doesn't fit the sentence's contrast. **(B)** matches the prediction. The trap choices are exactly the everyday meanings.

question.question: Best first move on a Words-in-Context question?
options: Predict a word from the sentence's logic before reading choices
Pick the most common meaning of the word
question.explanation: Predicting from context first inoculates you against the SAT's favorite trap: the word's familiar-but-here-wrong sense.

question.question: Diagnose the mistake.
question.scenario: On a 'purpose of this sentence' question, a student picks a choice that accurately *restates what the sentence says*. They get it wrong.

rubricCriteria.description: distinguishes what a sentence SAYS from what it DOES (its function)
notes purpose questions need a functional verb (to counter/illustrate/qualify…)
recommends naming the sentence's job in the paragraph, not paraphrasing it

question.explanation: Purpose ≠ paraphrase. A choice can correctly summarize the sentence yet not name its *role*; that's the credited trap on structure/purpose items.

hints: Did Author 2 deny X works, or limit when it works?
slides.workedSolution: Cross-text answers hinge on stance precision: short-term-only evidence *qualifies* (accepts with a limit) rather than *rejects* (denies outright) or *agrees* (no reservation). Naming the stance verb picks the answer.

question.question: Two paired texts: Author 1 argues policy X works; Author 2 presents data that X works only short-term. Author 2 would most likely:
options: Qualify Author 1's claim, accepting it with an added limitation
question.explanation: "Works only short-term" concedes the effect but bounds it — a qualification, not a rejection or full agreement.

question.question: "Purpose" questions are best answered with:
options: A verb naming what the text does (qualify, counter, illustrate)
A summary of the text's content
question.explanation: Function is a verb. If you can say the sentence's job, the right option is the one matching that verb.

question.prompt: Teach back: why does 'predict, then match' beat 'read the choices first' on Words-in-Context — and what trap does it defeat?

rubricCriteria.description: prediction is built from the sentence's own logic/cues
matching to a prediction resists the familiar-but-wrong-sense trap
reading choices first primes you toward the common meaning

question.question: In your own words, state the difference between what a sentence *says* and what it *does*, with one example.

rubricCriteria.description: 'does' = its function in the paragraph (a verb role)
gives a concrete example distinguishing the two

slides.title: How it scores & what's next
slides.body: Craft & Structure is ~28% of Reading & Writing. Reading for *function* here sets up **Expression of Ideas** next, where you become the author — choosing the sentence that best achieves a stated rhetorical goal.
